profile.summary: Ecclesiastes presents a profound and realistic reflection on life from the perspective of biblical wisdom. The book starts from the tension between the fleetingness of all that exists and the possibility of a life with purpose before God. The Preaster observes time, work, pleasure, injustice, wisdom and human limitations, insisting that earthly achievements do not offer lasting meaning in themselves. Still, the book does not lead to despair: the proper answer is to fear God, to keep his commandments, to remember the Creator and to receive with gratitude the gifts of life while living under his rule and in the light of the final judgment.
profile.setting: The background suggested by the introduction is the period of prosperity and peace in Israel after the consolidation of the kingdom of David, when Solomon expanded culture, trade, diplomacy, agriculture and buildings, including cities, fortresses and the temple. In this environment of stability and material wealth, wisdom was valued and there was room for literary and public reflection. The introduction treats authorship as traditionally associated with Solomon, because the text describes him as king, son of David and Preactor; at the same time, he recognizes the presence of an editor who frames the words of the book with prologue and epilogue. The date and final form of the book are not treated as totally certain in the introduction, but the literary setting is linked to Israel's sapiential universe.

structure.label: Editorial Prologue
structure.description: Brief opening that presents the framing of the book and the main voice of the Preacher.

structure.label: Speeches of the Preagador
structure.description: The central body in which the Preactor examines the value of life, the brevity of existence and themes such as work, time, pleasure, wisdom and injustice under the sovereign rule of God.

structure.label: Editorial conclusion
structure.description: Closure of the book with the final synthesis: to fear God, to obey his commandments and to remember divine judgment.

themes: The brevity and the transience of life
The quest for meaning before God
Fear of God and responsibility in judgment
readingKeys: Notice how the book repeatedly returns to the idea that everything is passenger and does not support last meaning in itself.
Note the tension between the apparent futility of human experience and the assertion that God rules everything for purpose.
Read the end as an interpretative key: the reflection of the book leads to obedience, the fear of the Lord and the wise use of the gifts of life.
profile.cautions: The introduction presented assumes the traditional connection of the book with Solomon, but also highlights the mediation of an editor; therefore, it is worth mentioning this authorship cautiously, as probable and traditional, not as absolute certainty. The book should not be read as a denial of the goodness of life, but as a diagnosis of human limitation in a world marked by brevity, injustice and uncertainty. His final message is not cynicism, but reverence, obedience, and wisdom before God.

dossier.narratedEra: The setting presented in the notes situates Ecclesiastes in the period of peace and prosperity after the conquests of David, when Solomon rules and Israel lives his golden years (1 Rs 4:34; 10:23-24; 2 Cr 5:2-7:7, as quoted by the notes). The book, however, is presented as a discourse of "the Precator" within this royal setting, not as an account of a continuous historical event.
dossier.compositionEra: The notes treat composition as traditionally linked to Solomon, identified by various titles and internal indications (1:1, 12, 16; 2:7, 9), but Matthew Henry emphasizes that the book is a preaching written in literary form and that it may reflect a later period of Solomon's life after his apostasy and recovery, when he is already old (cf. 12:1-14). Thus, the salomonic setting and the writing date should not be confused.

politics.title: Peaceful Kingdom after David
politics.detail: The notes place the scene in Israel during a period of peace and stability after David had established his empire. Solomon acts in a consolidated kingdom rather than an expansionist war context.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read Ecclesiastes as a reflection of a king in times of administration, prosperity and order, not as a discourse shaped by immediate military crisis.

politics.title: Solomon as king, wise and probable traditional author
politics.detail: The text is traditionally attributed to Solomon because the Preasury is described as the son of David and king, and the notes say that these titles strongly point to him.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains royal and didactic weight: the book sounds like wisdom offered by someone with experience of government, wealth and public influence.

politics.title: David as a dynastic reference, not narrative focus
politics.detail: The notes mention David as Solomon's father and as a reference for the identification of the Preactor, but do not develop any specific dynastic conflict within Ecclesiastes.
politics.readingImpact: It is avoided to read the book as a narrative of the Davidic court itself; the weight falls upon the authority of the king-wise and his instruction.

politics.title: Diplomacy and international reception of wisdom
politics.detail: Tyndale notes that kings and ambassadors came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and that he developed international trade, diplomacy and agriculture.
politics.readingImpact: This reinforces that the book can be read as wisdom with public circulation and interest beyond Israel, not just as a private reflection.
politics.reference: Introduction of Ecclesiastes, "Author and Recipients" and "Setting"; cf. 1 Rs 4:34; 10:23-24

customs.title: Public assembly and sapiential teaching
customs.detail: The term "Pregador" is linked to the idea of someone who brings together an assembly. The notes suggest that the content may have been publicly proclaimed before leaders and representatives of tribes, on a solemn occasion.
customs.readingImpact: Reading Ecclesiastes as public discourse highlights their tone of exhortation and practical application, not just private meditation.

customs.title: Cut life and servants before the king
customs.detail: Matthew Henry describes the listeners as Solomon's happy "servants," who remained continually before him to hear his wisdom.
customs.readingImpact: This colores the book as court instruction: wisdom transmitted to people exposed to administration, honor and responsibility.

customs.title: Work, administration and practical utility
customs.detail: Tyndale points out that the Preagador deals with work, wisdom and pleasure, and that his reflection reaches ordinary administrators and citizens who need to navigate everyday life.
customs.readingImpact: Reading ceases to be abstract: the text speaks of work routines, practical decisions and limits of human activity under the rule of God.

customs.title: Economy of prosperity, trade and public works
customs.detail: The scenario notes mention material prosperity, international trade, cities, fortresses and the Temple, as well as agriculture as part of Solomon's national advance.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to understand why Ecclesiastes can speak of wealth, achievements and human works: it is born in a context of abundance and great projects.

customs.title: Burial and social honor as limited goods
customs.detail: In 6:3-6, the notes mention the importance of old age, descent, and a worthy burial, contrasting this with the tragedy of an unhiked life.
customs.readingImpact: Social honor appears as insufficient to ensure meaning; reading is shaped by concrete values of family, longevity and funeral in the ancient world.

customs.title: Use of perfumes/aphrodisiacs and references to sexuality
customs.detail: At 12:5, the caperberry is identified as aphrodisiac known in the ancient Near East.
customs.readingImpact: This illuminates the description of aging: the final poem uses a concrete and culturally recognizable body image to show the loss of vigor.

language.title: hebel as "vapor", "fôlego" or transience
language.detail: The notes state that the central term translated "coo/unsno sense" is hebel, literally "breathing, steam."
language.readingImpact: The word does not need to be read only as "absurd"; it emphasizes escape, volatility, and inability to hold life in our hands.

language.title: Under the sun's as a earthly perspective
language.detail: Tyndale notes that the expression often occurs in Ecclesiastes and suggests a vision of life limited to the earth, in contrast to God's perspective.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the Preagador often describes the human experience from the point of view of the observed world, not as a denial of divine sovereignty.

language.title: Circular and repetitive structure of discourse
language.detail: In 1:2-11, the section is described as moved by circular rhythms of coming and going, and the literary arrangement itself mirrors this circularity.
language.readingImpact: The form of the text reinforces the content: repetition is not defective, but part of the argument about the repetition and brevity of existence.

language.title: Image of the wind as a metaphor of evasivity
language.detail: "Raining behind the wind" is explained as something that goes and comes quickly, like life itself.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor helps to read the book's complaints as a concrete experience of uselessness of human effort when separated from God.

language.title: Poem in prose and metaphors of aging
language.detail: In 12:1-7, the notes describe a "bealog prosa" poem with many Hebrew metaphors about the decline of old age.
language.readingImpact: The end of the book must be read poetically, not merely literallyistic; the collective image communicates human fragility and spiritual urgency.

language.title: -Cacete with tips and painful discipline
language.detail: In 12:11, the notes explain the image of the aguillons and stakes as painful lessons that direct us to paths that we would not choose.
language.readingImpact: Language suggests that wisdom can be incisive and corrective, not just comforting.

timeline.title: Was of peace and splendor under Solomon
timeline.detail: The setting is placed after David, at the height of peace and prosperity of the united kingdom, when Solomon promotes culture, commerce and great works.
timeline.readingImpact: The book is read as wisdom produced in a period of maximum national experience, when the question for the meaning of life arises despite prosperity.

timeline.title: Solomon as a traditional author and wise king
timeline.detail: The notes link the Preacher to the title of King and the Son of Davi, and Matthew Henry suggests that observations may come from the maturity of Solomon's life.
timeline.readingImpact: Reading gains internal chronology: the discourse may reflect the final phase of Solomon's life, when he already has broad experience and repentance.

timeline.title: Apostasy and recovery of Solomon as an interpretative frame
timeline.detail: Matthew Henry mentions Solomon's late apostasy and assumes that Ecclesiastes is a sermon of repentance, written after his fall and restoration by grace.
timeline.readingImpact: This makes the book read as a testimony of spiritual experience, not just as a sapiential theory.
timeline.reference: Introduction of Matthew Henry; cf. 1 Rs 11:1

timeline.title: Summary of the book in two editorial frames
timeline.detail: Tyndale states that the book is framed by a very brief prologue (1:1) and an epilogue/conclusion (12:9-14).
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should pay attention to the editor's voice and interpretative closure, especially 12:13-14.

timeline.title: Memory, forgetfulness and human limit
timeline.detail: In 1:11, the notes affirm that we cannot count on the remembrance of what we have done; human life and its deeds pass without guarantee of permanence.
timeline.readingImpact: The temporality of the book gains strength: human experience is marked by social forgetfulness and the brevity of fame.

timeline.title: Final poem on aging and powder return
timeline.detail: In 12:7, the body returns to dust and the spirit returns to God, echoing Genesis.
timeline.readingImpact: The closing of the book shifts the discussion of "vapor" to concrete mortality and responsibility before God.

investigation: The secondary source speaks repeatedly of Solomon, but does not historically resolve the final authorship; Tyndale's introduction treats attribution as strong, and Matthew Henry as a frame of repentance and maturity, which is a devotional reading and not an independent historical proof.
Notes do not offer an exact chronology of writing, so any accurate date remains not demonstrated here.
There is mention of possible public discourse before leaders and ambassadors, but this is inferred from 2 Cr 5:2-7:7 and 1 Rs 4:34; 10:23-24, not directly described as the occasion of Ecclesiastes.
The editorial structure of the book is accepted in the notes (prologue and epilogue), but the weight and exact function of internal voices remain interpretive theme.
The comments on caperberry, the poem of aging and the metaphor of the grave are specific, but selective; they do not cover all the cultural images of the book.
The notes make pastoral and confessional use of Ecclesiastes, especially in 12:13-14, then the dossier reflects a Protestant evangelical perspective without extrapolating beyond the sources provided.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, which are devotional/explanatory introductions and comments, not independent historical studies. Therefore, several statements appear only as tradition or interpretation, especially about Solomon, his apostasy, his recovery and the possible public occasion of the speech. The coverage is selective: it focused on the themes explained in the notes on Ecclesiastes 1, 6 and 12 and the general introduction. No gaps were filled with external data, and no chronologies, political geography or unmentioned customs were not attempted. There are also internal tensions between a traditional reading of salomonic authorship and the editorial distinction between "Pregador" and "editor"; these tensions were preserved rather than artificially harmonized.
